Viren Patel, a franchise operator who has run restaurants under two other national brands, has signed a franchise agreement to open The Flying Biscuit Café in Greenville, N.C. The agreement covers one café, the brand’s first in eastern North Carolina. Site selection is underway, and an opening date will be announced once a lease is signed. Patel is the franchisee and sole owner of the Greenville café. He holds a master’s degree in chemistry and spent roughly eight years as a multi-unit restaurant franchisee in Canada, running five locations, before moving to the United States in 2015 and buying into gas station and lodging businesses. Flying Biscuit is his first restaurant brand as an owner, and he plans to work in the café day to day. Greenville is the health care, education and commercial hub of eastern North Carolina. The Greenville metro area grew 6.5% between 2020 and 2025, from 173,642 residents to an estimated 182,936, according to U.S. Census Bureau estimates — among the fastest growth rates of any metro in the state. East Carolina University enrolled 27,153 students and employed 6,230 people in fall 2025, its highest enrollment since 2021. ECU Health, headquartered in Greenville, is an academic health system serving more than 1.4 million people across 29 eastern North Carolina counties. Flying Biscuit cafés serve breakfast and lunch only, closing at 3 p.m., a daypart Patel said drew him to the brand. “My daughter is the one who pointed out that we live in the South and this is Southern breakfast done right,” said Viren Patel, Flying Biscuit Café franchisee for Greenville. “I ate at Flying Biscuit six or seven times before I ever filled out an application. Greenville has students, young families, people coming off shift at the hospital and retirees. I want a place where all of them end up at the same tables on a Saturday morning.” Patel said he compared Flying Biscuit against independent breakfast concepts and other franchised cafés before signing, and that the brand’s menu range was the deciding factor. He hopes to add locations in his region over the next five years and has expressed interest in Fayetteville and Jacksonville, N.C., as possible markets beyond his current agreement. “North Carolina has become one of our deeper states, and Greenville is exactly the kind of market we want next — a university, a hospital system and a lot of people who are up early,” said Andrew Scherzer, partner and director of franchise development for Flying Biscuit Franchising. “Viren has run franchised restaurants for other brands and businesses that were entirely his own, so he knows what each one asks of you. He wants to run this one himself, and Greenville is going to get an owner who knows his regulars by name.” A site, opening timeline, café size and hiring plans will be announced once a lease is signed. The Greenville agreement follows a run of recent signings and openings. In North Carolina, Tahir Rafiq and his wife and franchise partner, Zinnia Tahir, signed a lease in North Raleigh for their fourth Flying Biscuit, targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Chris Compton opened his second café in downtown Knoxville, Tenn., on Sept. 12, after opening the brand’s first Tennessee location in 2025. The brand signed its first Missouri lease in St. Charles, outside St. Louis, in August, the first step under a development agreement covering three cafés. Matt Thomas signed a two-café development agreement for Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sept. 11, and agreements were signed for Nashville and the Tri-Cities region of Tennessee earlier this fall. Prospective operators can review available territories, investment requirements and the steps to begin a conversation at flyingbiscuitfranchising.com, or call the franchise sales line at 678-726-1884. articles.title: Applauding the Wrong Thing: The High Cost of Hero Culture in Restaurants
articles.titleKo: Applauding the Wrong Thing: The High Cost of Hero Culture in Restaurants
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Every time I keynote or run a workshop, I stay for the recognition part of the event. The awards, the promotions, the moment somebody gets called up in front of everybody they work with. I’ve sat through dozens of these, and I clap as loud as anybody in the room, because I know what it took that person to get up there. But somewhere along the way I started listening to the words instead of just clapping along to them. And the words are almost always the same. The person we were celebrating was always at the location. They were always on call. They always picked up the phone. They were the first one in and the last one out. They worked harder and were more dedicated than anybody else on the team. Everybody stands. Everybody claps. I clap too, because those are real sacrifices and that person earned the moment. Then I started watching the room instead of the stage. That’s where it got uncomfortable. The Two Thoughts Running Through the Room While that manager is up there holding the plaque, there are two very specific thoughts running through the people watching, and I’ve had enough managers tell me about them afterward that I know I’m not guessing. The first one comes from the manager who’s already stretched thin. There’s no way they work harder than I do. There’s no way they’re at that location more than I am. So what am I missing here? Am I just not being seen? The second one is worse. It comes from the manager who’s trying to hold some kind of line between work and home. How much more do I have to give up to be next? What am I trading for it? Which of my kid’s games, which dinners, which Sundays? Is that actually what it costs here? Neither one of those is inspiring. Both of them are quiet. Nobody raises a hand and says it out loud. But they walk out of that ballroom inside somebody’s head, and they sit there for months. We spent 90 seconds celebrating somebody, and in those same 90 seconds we told everybody else in that room exactly what the price of admission is. What We’re Actually Rewarding Take the honest read on what a lot of those awards measure. We’re rewarding attendance, we’re rewarding availability, and we’re rewarding somebody’s willingness to hand their personal boundaries over to the operation. Those are real contributions and I’m not minimizing them, because I’ve been that guy and so have you. But that’s not the same thing as leadership, and it’s damn sure not the same thing as coaching. But think about what we’re actually saying out loud when we read those qualities off a card. If a manager is always at the location, the team was never developed well enough to run without them. If a manager is always on call, nobody ever built the systems to protect their off hours. If a manager was first in and last out, nobody else on that team was ever trusted with an open or a close. That’s not a leadership story. That’s a fragility story, and we’re handing out plaques for it. What It Costs the Person on Stage There’s another layer to this that nobody says out loud, and I know it because I’ve been the one holding the plaque. Years back I was on the edge of leaving a brand for these exact reasons. I was traveling the country nonstop. I’d built the training systems for the new hires coming in at my level, and then I mentored them. I said yes to every special project that came across my desk. Always available, always there. And I was done. So I’d started interviewing somewhere else. That brand had its annual event that year, the kind you don’t miss. And I’m standing out in the hallway on my phone with a recruiter, working out the schedule for my third round of interviews. My boss is in the doorway of the conference room waving me in. I can see him. I know I need to go. I hold up a finger and keep talking, because that call mattered more to me right then than whatever was happening in that room. I hung up.

articles.title: Papa Murphy’s Owner MTY Group Turns Focus Inward as Strategic Review Comes to a Close

articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Wide-ranging operator MTY Group this past quarter concluded a strategic review that began a year ago in November. At the outset, it included, among a bevy of options, the potential sale of all or part of the company. That won’t happen, MTY Group announced Friday during its Q3 review, as a special committee of independent directors and the board elected to “accelerate the evolution of MTY’s current strategic plan, with a sharpened focus on efficiency, simplification, and disciplined capital allocation.” However, this doesn’t mean MTY, which directs Kahala Brands and its 28-plus concepts (like Cold Stone, Blimpie, Pinkberry, and Wetzel’s), as well as BBQ Holdings (Famous Dave’s, Village Inn, and nine others), and Papa Muphy’s, alongside a host of Canadian concepts such as Mr. Sub and Thai Express (the company is based north of the border), isn’t looking at its portfolio. CEO Eric Lefebvre told investors “everything is for sale if the price is right.” “But there’s no strong desire to divest of good brands,” he explained. “… Every brand will need to be evaluated for its potential and for the plan we have to make it grow. And the brands we might decide … are no longer relevant might not necessarily be the underperforming brands.” It could, Lefebvre added, be concepts MTY doesn’t have plans for or can’t come up with value creation. “But yes,” he said, “I would expect that more underperforming brands will be discussed than the top brands that are performing well.” MORE: Papa Murphy’s to Close Up to 50 Restaurants At Q3’s close, MTY’s fleet covered 6,966 locations, of which 6,782 were franchised or under operator agreements and 184 corporate. Fifty-seven percent were housed in the U.S.; 35 percent in Canada; and 8 percent international. The company opened 72 stores and closed 146. Fifty shuttered locations were related to a corporate closure announcement made last quarter. Company-run restaurants now comprise 2.6 percent of MTY’s network versus 3.6 percent a year ago—an effort it’s continuing. Additionally, 27 new stores slated for Q3 pushed into Q4 thanks to “various uncontrollable delays.” Regarding the company-run closure note, Lefebvre said, he expects the bulk of one-time costs to realize over the coming two quarters, with benefits from stripping underperforming units surfacing the ensuing period, including an estimated $2.5 million benefit. The company identified seven more restaurants it expects to go dark on top of 68 it guided previously to bring the total to 75. As shared, 50 have already closed. Most were repossessed stores (restaurants MTY bought from franchisees hoping to improve) and a few stemmed from acquisitions over recent years. For instance, a Papa Murphy’s portfolio MTY took over two years ago. Eventually, the company came to the realization those stores weren’t going to reroute. Simply, some regions were more damaged than anticipated. “The rationalization of corporate stores marks an important step for the company in our pursuit of value creation, growth and taking decisive action,” Lefebvre said. MTY’s Q3 system sales were essentially steady, year-over-year, at $1.5 billion and same-store sales decreased 1.9 percent. Canada was flat; the U.S. slid 2.7 percent; and international dropped 9.1 percent. Lefebvre said MTY’s strategic review, initiated November 17, 2025, resulted in conversations with a “range of interested parties” and the company considered a broad set of options. It generated interest among potential investors and reaffirmed, he said, the “strength, resilience, and strategic value of MTY’s platform.” Part of optimizing the company’s suite of brands will be to keep reverting to an asset-light franchising model. articles.title: I’m donut ? Now Delivering in NYC
articles.titleKo: I’m donut ? Now Delivering in NYC
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . I’m donut ?, the Tokyo-born cult-favorite donut shop, is now offering delivery to Manhattanites. This marks the first time that the brand has ever offered delivery anywhere in the world — giving fans unprecedented access to its coveted treats without the infamous storefront wait times. Since its inception by Chef Ryouta Hirako, I’m donut ? has drawn hours-long queues across Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia and New York’s Times Square for their signature nama donuts – light, melt-in-your-mouth creations unavailable anywhere else in the U.S. Now, these world-renowned pastries are more accessible than ever, with fans able to have I’m donut ? delivered right to their doorstep. The delivery menu features a selection of best-selling donuts for à la carte ordering: signature nama donuts (Original, Matcha, Chocolate); vegan ring donuts (Glazed, Strawberry Chocolate, Pistachio White Chocolate); savory donuts (NY BLT, Chicken Ginger Teriyaki, Scrambled Eggs); and specialty donuts (Zaku Zaku, Choco Shell). Signature beverages are also available for delivery, including Matcha and Hojicha options served iced or hot, and specialty drinks like the Salted Maple Hojicha Latte, Classic Hot Chocolate, and housemade lemonade. Exclusive to online ordering is a Half-Dozen Box Set, which features the I’m donut ? Original, Matcha, Choco Shell, Zaku-Zaku, Glazed, and Strawberry Chocolate. Also available is the limited-edition Treat Yourself Box, which includes the I’m donut ? Original, Choco Shell, and Glazed, as well as Lunch Combos, which come with a choice of the NY BLT or Ginger Chicken Teriyaki and a beverage. The post I’m donut ? articles.title: Pret A Manger Relaunches Coffee Subscription with Major Perks
articles.titleKo: Pret A Manger Relaunches Coffee Subscription with Major Perks
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Americans love their specialty drinks, whether it’s a morning latte, an afternoon matcha or a flavored iced tea. Now, Pret A Manger (Pret) is making that ritual a lot more rewarding with the relaunch of Club Pret, its monthly subscription that goes beyond a simple coffee order. Members get up to five Barista-made drinks a day, including all matcha drinks, 20% off the full Pret menu and unlimited drink customizations at no additional cost. “We’ve given Club Pret a serious upgrade, with more value and more flexibility in how you enjoy your daily Pret fix, so we wanted to celebrate with a club night of our own,” said Felipe Athayde, President of North America, Pret A Manger. “For one night only, we’re turning our Union Square shop into an actual club, complete with a DJ plus espresso and matcha martinis. The party lasts one night, but the perks keep coming every day.” Open to everyone, the event will take place on Friday, October 23, from 6 to 9 p.m. ET at Pret’s Union Square shop at 857 Broadway. Guests will walk a red carpet before heading upstairs to the Club Pret lounge, where a live DJ as well as espresso and matcha martinis will set the mood. Outside the Union Square shop, Pret will unveil a new mural by New York artist Frank Ape (Brandon Sines), whose joyful Sasquatch character has become a fixture of the city’s street-art scene, appearing in projects across the city. The mural features a collection of Pret drinks, offering a playful visual nod to Club Pret’s refreshed benefits. Club Pret members and guests who join at the event will receive a limited-edition Pret x Frank Ape tote, while supplies last. To redeem their free tote, members will need to show their active Club Pret subscription in the Pret app upon entry to the event. Frank will be on-site to sign the totes, five of which will contain a golden key redeemable for one complimentary year of Club Pret membership. Club Pret members can choose from organic coffees, teas, lattes, hot chocolates and newly added matcha drinks, served hot or iced, in any size and with any milk or plant-based milk. Every drink can be customized with unlimited add-ons such as syrups, compotes and extra espresso shots. At $50 per month, Club Pret works out to less than $2 per day for up to five drinks per day, and new members can get their first month free. For additional information on Club Pret, visit https://www.pret.com/en-US/club-pret . The post Pret A Manger Relaunches Coffee Subscription with Major Perks appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: How AI is Changing Quick-Service Restaurant Ordering in 2026
articles.titleKo: How AI is Changing Quick-Service Restaurant Ordering in 2026
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The technology has promise in mobile applications, websites, drive-thru systems and other ordering channels. Artificial intelligence is playing an ever-increasing role in the quick service restaurant ordering experience. AI is changing the way customers find menu items, place orders and interact with restaurants, from personalized recommendations and conversational ordering to predictive technology. The technology is moving beyond the experimentation phase for QSR operators. AI is being integrated by ordering platforms to make transactions faster, more personalized, and easier to manage. Personalized Ordering Experiences Personalization is one of the most visible applications of AI in restaurant ordering. Artificial intelligence can help to give more relevant recommendations by looking at previous orders, preferences, time of day and purchasing patterns, as opposed to giving every customer the same menu experience. For example, when opening a restaurant ordering platform, a customer who regularly orders vegetarian dishes might see relevant menu items highlighted. If a customer regularly buys a combination, they might get suggestions for what else to add to their usual order . AI-Powered Conversational Ordering Conversational interfaces powered by AI are transforming the way customers engage with restaurant ordering systems. Instead of navigating through multiple menu categories, customers can express their needs in plain language. A customer could ask for a meal with certain ingredients, ask what options are available or change an existing order, all through a conversational interface. This technology can help QSRs simplify the ordering journey while creating another channel for customers who prefer conversational interactions versus traditional app navigation. Smarter Recommendations and Upselling AI may also help QSRs to offer more relevant upselling recommendations. Traditional upselling usually relies on predefined combinations or generic recommendations, but artificial intelligence can offer more contextual suggestions. For example, a burger order might be accompanied by a recommendation based on combinations that people tend to order together. Recommendations also can be based on past purchasing behavior. Voice and AI-Assisted Ordering Voice technology is another growing channel for ordering restaurants. Customers can order via AI-driven voice interfaces, without having to manually navigate through menus. The technology has promise in mobile applications, websites, drive-thru systems and other ordering channels. Outside of drive-thru operations, AI-assisted voice ordering might help fulfilll routine requests while employees attend to other duties. But it’s all about accuracy after all. Voice technology is convenient, but it can be easily undermined by misinterpretations of customisations or incorrect orders. Predictive Technology Behind the Scenes The role of AI does not end with the submission of the order. Predictive technology can help restaurants to forecast ordering patterns and prepare for changes in demand. Historical ordering data can reveal patterns around busy times, popular menu items, and seasonal demand. Such insights can help to better prepare and avoid the lack of availability of popular items in peak periods. For multi-location QSR operators, these insights can also assist in better planning of operations. Faster Customer Support AI is increasingly being used to assist customers after they place an order. Frequent questions about order status, estimated delivery times, menu availability, and other routine concerns can be answered with automated systems. When deployed properly, AI-powered support offers immediate answers and allows human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. articles.title: Your Restaurant Doesn’t Need Another App. It Needs an Intelligent Experience Engine
articles.titleKo: Your Restaurant Doesn’t Need Another App. It Needs an Intelligent Experience Engine
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . As AI expands what digital platforms can do, the restaurants that create the strongest experience won’t necessarily introduce the most features. The restaurant industry’s approach to mobile has largely followed the same playbook: ordering, payments, loyalty and promotions. Each solves a need, but checking those boxes does not necessarily create a better customer experience. As digital becomes a bigger part of how guests interact with their favorite restaurants, brands should be asking a bigger question: How can technology make every interaction more relevant without losing what made customers love the brand in the first place? That requires thinking beyond the app as a transaction tool and toward an intelligent experience engine that can learn from how customers interact with the brand and evolve alongside them. Digital should strengthen the rituals, preferences and human interactions that build loyalty, not replace them. Start with the experience, not the feature list Digital product development often begins with “What should the app do?” Mobile ordering? Personalized offers? Or even worse, “What can my existing systems do?” The starting point should be the customer. What brings someone back? Where does friction exist? What makes the brand distinct? Which parts of that experience can technology make easier or more relevant, and which should remain distinctly human? In our work with a fast-growing coffee brand with a highly engaged customer base, the opportunity wasn’t simply to recreate the physical experience on a smaller screen. It was to consider how a digital platform could support the behaviors and rituals that made the brand distinctive while creating a foundation that could evolve. Rather than rely on old assumptions about mobile ordering apps, we reset around what the ideal customer experience. Strategic technology investments followed from that view of the experience, not the other way around. Having customer data isn’t the same as knowing your customer Restaurants already generate valuable signals about customer behavior. What someone orders, when they order, which location they visit, and how often they return. Yet, a restaurant can have years of transaction history and still deliver a generic experience. The opportunity lies in connecting those signals to make each interaction useful. AI can identify patterns across ordering behavior, preference, location, and timing to make repeat orders easier, surface relevant menu information or adapt to different occasions. But none of that happens simply because a restaurant “adds AI.” If ordering data, loyalty information, and customer preferences are siloed, an intelligent layer can only do so much. Connected systems, sound data architecture and scalable product engineering are what make a more responsive experience possible. That coffee brand, for example, was replacing its entire technology stack during the engagement, moving to a new point-of-sale platform, payment processor, loyalty provider and marketing cloud at the same time. Delivering the experience required a ground-up point-of-sale integration and a purpose-built menu translation layer that carries the in-store menu into the digital ordering experience. Bounteous has since made that layer a reusable asset, so other brands can connect a different point-of-sale system without rebuilding the integration from scratch. Personalization should feel like recognition, not automation Too often, personalization means another offer or notification designed to prompt a purchase. The best restaurant experiences have always been more human: a regular walk in and someone knows their order, or an employee recommends something they might enjoy. articles.titleKo: AMMA & ATTA Brings Ayurvedic-Inspired Food, Drinks And Wellness To Canary Wharf
articles.originalSummary: AMMA & ATTA has launched its first concept at Market Halls Canary Wharf for a three-month residency. The new brand combines nourishing daytime food and botanical drinks, bringing Ayurvedic wisdom into the modern day. Ganan Kanagathurai, Owner Roti King & ex CEO Itsu is working with the new venture as its strategic adviser, and comments: “Amma & Atta brings something truly thoughtful to the table. By pairing ancient wisdom with modern nutritional science, they’ve created vibrant, comforting food that leaves you genuinely energised. It’s nourishing, full of flavour, and a wonderful reflection of where modern dining is heading.” Designed around the realities of modern life, AMMA & ATTA recognises that how we feel and what we need can shift throughout the day. Sometimes your day asks you to energise, sometimes to find your centre, and sometimes simply to slow down. Through food, drinks and simple everyday rituals, AMMA & ATTA creates moments in the day to help you do just that. The concept brings this to life through three energies: RISE, ALIGN and RETURN. RISE is designed to energise, ALIGN to balance and RETURN to ground. Customers are invited to ask: Which do you need today? Choose your ritual. From wealth management to nourishment AMMA & ATTA was founded by Simone Hundle following a 25-year career in wealth management, including senior roles at JPMorgan and Citigroup. Her experience of corporate life led her to explore a different approach to balance, wellbeing and nourishment, bringing her to holistic healing and Ayurveda, which became a foundation for the brand. “I know what it feels like to work in an environment that can be incredibly fast-paced and stressful, moving from one meeting to the next and grabbing something to eat without really stopping or thinking about what you need. “For me, food and nutrition are a form of care, giving us an opportunity to pause and reconnect. That idea also has a very personal meaning. Amma means mother and Atta means flour. After my husband lost his parents, making parathas became a way for him to stay connected to his mother and his Punjabi childhood, and something that brought our own family around the table. That idea of food, family and care is reflected in the brand’s signature: Made by Mother.” Simone combines her commercial experience with qualifications as a Holistic Healing Counsellor and Ayurvedic Lifestyle and Nutrition Consultant. Ancient wisdom, contemporary food The food at AMMA & ATTA draws on Indian home cooking, with a particular focus on Punjabi cuisine, while Ayurveda informs the ingredients, combinations and preparation. The menu is organised around three energies: RISE, ALIGN and RETURN, drawing inspiration from the Ayurvedic doshas Kapha, Pitta and Vata. Traditionally used in Ayurveda to describe different qualities of body and mind, the doshas provide a framework for the menu and the experience. The format has been developed for health-conscious professionals and families seeking nourishing, convenient and high-quality food and drinks throughout the day. The Canary Wharf menu brings this to life with morning dishes including Kitchari, Turmeric & Beetroot Granola and Apple & Cinnamon Porridge; all-day warm spelt paratha rolls filled with Chicken, Avocado & Gunpowder or Paneer; and warm chaat-inspired bowls built around dal, chickpeas and kitchari, layered with vegetables and protein and finished with Hari’s freshly made coriander chutney, sweet tamarind, pomegranate, fresh coriander and sev. The menu is complemented by botanical shots, Ayurvedic-inspired teas, Amma’s Chai and a Turmeric & Ashwagandha Latte. Botanical drinks The drinks range extends the same Ayurvedic-inspired approach beyond the food. Three Ayurvedic-inspired botanical teas offer a bright blend for RISE, a refreshing blend for ALIGN and a warming blend for RETURN, each bringing together seven carefully curated herbs and botanicals. articles.title: Langan’s Brasserie Celebrates 50 Years with One-Day-Only Anniversary Event at 1976 Prices
articles.titleKo: Langan’s Brasserie Celebrates 50 Years with One-Day-Only Anniversary Event at 1976 Prices
articles.originalSummary: Set to be Langan’s Brasserie’ s biggest night of the year, the iconic Mayfair restaurant will be hosting a celebration whereby guests can enjoy a specially curated 50th Anniversary Menu for one night only. Not only will the menu feature much-loved Langan’s classics, but they can all be enjoyed for prices not seen since 1976. Taking place on Tuesday 20th October, the Mayfair institution will open its doors from 11am through to late, inviting guests to experience a full day of nostalgic dining and celebration. The brasserie will set the tone with a live pianist, creating a classic Langan’s atmosphere as guests dine on heritage dishes paired with half a bottle of wine per person, included as part of the experience. Alongside the main dining room, the upstairs space will be open throughout the day, offering a more relaxed setting with a slightly adjusted menu and pricing, ensuring the celebrations flow across the entire restaurant. In keeping with the spirit of the era, the drinks offering will also nod to the past, with cocktails such as the French ‘76, a sparkling serve made with cognac and champagne, alongside classics like the Cosmopolitan and Between the Sheets, all priced as they would have been in 1976. As the evening unfolds, the celebrations will transition into a lively afterparty, where a live band with three rotating singers will take to the stage before a DJ keeps the energy going late into the night – a fitting tribute to Langan’s long-standing reputation for hosting some of London’s most memorable parties. Tickets are priced at £35 to dine, with food and drinks available at original 1976 prices, making this a rare opportunity to step back in time and experience one of London’s most iconic restaurants as it was at the very beginning. Blending nostalgia with the signature flair that has defined Langan’s for five decades, the 50th anniversary event promises a day-to-night celebration of food, music and Mayfair glamour. Further information on bookings coming soon!

articles.title: Dave’s Hot Chicken Reaches 500 Locations
articles.titleKo: Dave’s Hot Chicken Reaches 500 Locations
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Dave’s Hot Chicken today announced the opening of its 500th restaurant in Phoenix, AZ, on October 8, marking another major milestone for a brand that began with three childhood friends, $900, portable fryers and folding tables in an East Hollywood parking lot less than a decade ago. What started in 2017 as a late-night pop-up quickly drew lines around the block, with an early Eater LA review helping fuel demand that soon outpaced the founders’ original plans. Rather than spending a year at the pop-up and another with a food truck, Dave’s made the leap to brick-and-mortar within months, eventually catching the attention of Wetzel’s Pretzels co-founder Bill Phelps, who partnered with the founders to begin franchising the concept nationwide. “When Dave, Tommy and I started this, we weren’t thinking about hundreds of restaurants. We were focused on making the best hot chicken we could and getting people to try it,” said Arman Oganesyan, co-founder of Dave’s Hot Chicken. “To see Dave’s reach 500 locations and become what it is today is hard to put into words. The scale has changed, but the energy and obsession with the food that got us started are still at the heart of who we are.” That early momentum has only accelerated. Dave’s reached its 400th restaurant earlier in 2026, with development maintaining an aggressive pace in the months that followed. Shortly after, the brand opened a record eight restaurants in a single day in April across markets from Connecticut to Utah. In total, Dave’s has added approximately 100 restaurants since reaching the 400-unit milestone, demonstrating the strength of its franchise system and its ability to execute at scale while maintaining the consistent guest experience that has fueled its rise. “Reaching 500 restaurants is an incredible milestone, especially when you consider where Dave’s started and how quickly the brand has grown,” said Jim Bitticks, CEO of Dave’s Hot Chicken. “That growth reflects the strength of our franchise partners, our operating model and the teams supporting these restaurants every day. We’re proud of the pace, but what matters most is continuing to grow the right way. As our footprint expands, we remain focused on disciplined execution and ensuring every restaurant delivers the same mind-blowing experience our guests expect from Dave’s.” Dave’s rapid climb to 500 restaurants has also taken the brand to some of the world’s most recognizable cities and destinations. Across the U.S., Dave’s has established a presence in major metropolitan markets from New York and Chicago to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, while increasingly taking the concept beyond traditional restaurant real estate and into major airports. Internationally, Dave’s has expanded across Canada and the Middle East and made its European debut with a high-profile flagship on London’s iconic Shaftesbury Avenue. That opening helped kick off a 60-restaurant development agreement across the U.K. and Ireland, and Dave’s has since expanded its partnership with Azzurri Group through an additional 180-restaurant agreement spanning 10 European countries, including France, Spain, Germany, Italy, Portugal and the Netherlands. With development rights sold for more than 1592 locations across globe, the brand is continuing to introduce its signature hot chicken to new markets and audiences around the world. Founded by Arman Oganesyan and classically trained chef Dave Kopushyan, along with brothers Tommy and Gary Rubenyan in early 2017, Dave’s Hot Chicken initially opened as a parking lot pop-up, with lines quickly wrapping around the block. Dave’s Hot Chicken offers a robust business model, including national and local marketing support, proven systems, manuals, operating procedures, and assistance with site selection. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Matcha has held its place in wellness rituals for centuries, and Robeks is giving guests a fresh, flavor-forward way to make it part of theirs. That’s the idea behind Robeks’ new Matcha Moments platform. Robeks, the go-to spot for creatively crafted fresh smoothies, juices, acai and smoothie bowls, artisan toasts and handheld bites, is introducing three new Matcha Moments flavors available in all stores beginning October 13. Built around Robeks’ new Supreme Matcha, Matcha Moments are designed to give guests the calm, steady lift matcha is loved for, wrapped in bold, craveable flavor. Matcha Moments arrives on the heels of Robeks’ Glow Smoothies platform, adding to the brand’s push toward lifestyle-driven wellness. Where Glow leaned into beauty and hydration, Matcha Moments taps into matcha’s reputation as one of the most functional ingredients in wellness today that is valued for its naturally occurring antioxidants and for delivering sustained energy and focus without the agitation or crash one can get from coffee. At the center of the platform is Supreme Matcha, a new premium matcha selected for its smooth, distinctive flavor. Robeks pairs it with bold fruit and flavor combinations that make matcha feel less like a wellness routine and more like a treat fans will crave. The three new Matcha Moments flavors are: – Mango Matcha Moment with Supreme Matcha, mango puree, and golden turmeric syrup. – Strawberry Matcha Moment with Supreme Matcha and strawberry puree. – Ube Matcha Moment with Supreme Matcha and ube powder. “Matcha has a reputation for calm, focused energy, and we wanted to build a platform that actually delivers on that while tasting incredible,” said David Hutchinson, vice president of marketing at Robeks. “With our new Matcha Moments, Robeks fans will get the antioxidants and steady lift matcha is known for, in flavors bold enough to make it their new go-to.” The platform arrives as matcha’s popularity continues to climb, driven by consumers looking for beverages that offer more than a caffeine boost. Matcha naturally contains L-theanine, an amino acid credited with its calm, focused energy, alongside catechins, a class of antioxidants in which matcha is especially rich. Robeks designed Matcha Moments to give guests an easy, everyday way to work those benefits into their routine, no ceremony required. In addition to Supreme Matcha, the platform introduces two new ingredients to the Robeks menu: golden turmeric syrup and ube powder, expanding the brand’s flavor lineup and giving guests new ways to experience matcha beyond its traditional preparation. Matcha Moments will be available at Robeks locations nationwide and through the Robeks Rewards app from October 13 through the end of the year. Ascension Coffee, a Dallas-based, women-led specialty coffee roaster and cafe group, opens its first Southlake cafe on Monday, Oct. 12 at 100 State St. in Southlake Town Square. The specialty coffee roaster will bring its signature coffees, chef-driven food and all-day hospitality to the 4,223-square-foot space, marking it as its largest location to date. “At Ascension, we’re intentional about every part of the experience, from the coffees we source and the food we serve to the relationships we build with our guests and our producer partners,” said Jessica Keenan, CEO of Ascension Coffee. “Opening our largest café in Southlake allows us to share that commitment on a larger scale, creating a place where people can gather throughout the day for coffee, food offerings, conversation, and connection. More than anything, we hope to become a meaningful part of the community and a welcoming third space woven into everyday life.” Ascension’s Southlake location will also feature the fall menu, which includes items that take a unique approach to seasonal flavors: Twilight Mocha : adaptogenic mushrooms, white and dark chocolate, oat milk and smoked sea salt Dotiki Apple Chai-der : doki, black tea, caramel, spices and ginger beer Crispy Hot Chicken Sammie : hand-breaded chicken thigh, spicy agave house slaw, roasted red pepper aioli and house pickles on brioche Apple Pie French Toast : croissant bread, house-made apple chutney, vanilla cream, cinnamon sugar and maple syrup. Ascension sources coffees produced by women, supporting greater economic opportunity and recognition for women across the coffee supply chain, with rotating single-origin selections available through the café’s slow bar. Ascension’s focus on community extends beyond the cafe. The company also worked with North Texas creatives on the Southlake cafe, including Dallas-based Tower Design Studio, which designed the interior, and Fort Worth artist Jan Riggins, who created a commissioned 3-D art installation for the space. Ascension will be holding a grand opening celebration on Thursday, Oct. 22, starting at 4:30 p.m., which will include a ribbon cutting with the Southlake Chamber of Commerce. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . SignalFlare AI today named restaurant technology veteran Robert Peterson as Chief Revenue Officer. Peterson will oversee sales, marketing, and partnerships as the company scales its AI-powered decision intelligence platform. “Robert knows how to scale technology across the restaurant industry. He’s done it many times.” said Mike Lukianoff, CEO of SignalFlare. “His experience at tech powerhouses NCR, PAR, Qu, and Oracle will accelerate our go-to-market efforts.” Peterson has spent more than two decades helping restaurant brands and their technology partners unlock value from transaction data. Most recently, he served as Area Vice President at Oracle Restaurants, where he brought digital transaction platforms to restaurant brands across North America. His expertise spans interoperability, open APIs, data standards, scalable adoption, and organizational change—capabilities that will help SignalFlare simplify integration and expand its impact. He serves on the Restaurant Technology Network (RTN) Vendor Advisory Council and was named an RTN Industry Champion in 2024 for his contributions to industry-defining restaurant data standards. Founded in 2023 to bring decision intelligence to restaurants, SignalFlare won Snowflake’s Startup Challenge in 2024, selected from more than 1,100 global entries. Since then, the company has evolved from a platform focused on price optimization into the leader in agentic decision intelligence for the restaurant industry. In March 2026, SignalFlare launched Navigator at the Multi-Unit Restaurant Technology Conference’ AI Summit. Navigator combines a proprietary contextual data set (mobile device data, credit card panel data, competitive item pricing, and hyperlocal economics) with each client’s own data to reveal the causes that POS data alone cannot explain. Built on a semantic layer and ontology, SignalFlare orchestrates 157 large language and frontier AI models to turn probabilistic AI into consistent, deterministic answers operators can trust. “For two decades, I have helped this industry collect and connect its transaction data to understand what happened in the business,” Peterson said. “But that was never enough. Operators always asked, ‘What do I do with that insight?’ SignalFlare provides the why, and what to do about it. We’re creating an entirely new category for restaurants: decision intelligence.” The post SignalFlare AI Names Robert Peterson as CRO appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: Report: Starbucks Exploring Takeover of Chipotle
articles.titleKo: Report: Starbucks Exploring Takeover of Chipotle
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Starbucks is led by CEO Brian Niccol, who previously oversaw Chipotle. Starbucks has reportedly explored acquiring Chipotle in what could become the largest takeover in restaurant industry history. According to the Financial Times , Starbucks has worked with advisers in recent months on a potential acquisition of the fast-casual chain. The status of those discussions remains unclear, including whether Starbucks has submitted a formal offer. The publication, citing people familiar with the matter, cautioned that a transaction of this magnitude would face significant challenges and may never materialize. Bloomberg also reported on the potential acquisition Thursday, noting that Chipotle shares surged as much as 8.6 percent following the news. Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.7 percent during trading, marking its largest intraday decline in more than a year. Starbucks declined to provide comment to the Financial Times. Chipotle did not immediately provide a comment in response to the Financial Times. The potential transaction would reunite Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with the company he led from 2018 until August 2024, when he departed to take over the coffee giant. Niccol spent more than six years transforming Chipotle into one of the industry’s most successful growth stories. His tenure included a significant expansion of digital ordering, the introduction of Chipotlanes, and a recovery from the food-safety challenges that had damaged the brand’s reputation. Since his departure, Chipotle’s stock has lost nearly half its value, according to the Financial Times. Starbucks operates roughly 41,000 company-owned and licensed stores globally, and Chipotle has more than 4,200 restaurants, the vast majority in the U.S. The deal would surpass Burger King’s $11.4 billion acquisition of Tim Hortons in 2014, which currently stands as the industry’s largest takeover. However, one analyst questioned the strategic rationale. “Initially, it doesn’t seem like there’s that many synergies for something like this to happen,” Melius Research analyst Jacob Aiken-Phillips told Bloomberg. “Obviously, Brian Niccol has intimate knowledge of Chipotle’s operations and Chipotle has pulled back a ton, but I’d have to hear a lot more about what the potential plan would be to see if there’s actually anything to be gained.” Aiken-Phillips suggested Chipotle’s supply chain could offer advantages as Starbucks continues expanding its food offerings. Chipotle’s established relationships with suppliers of fresh ingredients could provide purchasing opportunities, although the companies operate fundamentally different restaurant models. “Chipotle has purchasing scale of all these good, fresh ingredients and relationships across the country, so certainly that could help, but it’s not like Starbucks has a grill,” he told Bloomberg. Another analyst note from William Blair’s Sharon Zackfia suggested the financial case for a combination could be difficult to make. The analysis estimated potential corporate and technology savings at roughly $300 million, but saw limited traditional supply-chain overlap because Starbucks and Chipotle source fundamentally different products. Other possible benefits could include shared loyalty programs, cross-brand products, or using Starbucks’ international relationships to accelerate Chipotle’s licensed growth. Financing could be the larger hurdle. With Chipotle carrying an enterprise value above $40 billion, the analysis estimated a takeover could cost closer to $50 billion after factoring in a typical acquisition premium. The takeover speculation comes as the two chains navigate different stages of their respective turnarounds. articles.titleKo: Highland Brewing to Open Oscar’s Pizza, Honoring Founder and Oscar Wong
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Highland Brewing’s new restaurant, Oscar’s Pizza, will open on the brewery’s 40-acre Asheville campus this fall as a tasty tribute to Highland Brewing founder Oscar Wong. The pizzeria will soft open with a special event menu during the 30th Anniversary Cold Mountain weekend, Nov. 13–15, before officially opening with a more robust menu the week of Thanksgiving. Highland will celebrate Oscar’s Pizza with a grand opening event in December. As Highland’s 40-acre campus continues to evolve as a gathering place for beer, live music, outdoor recreation, and events, a food program inspired by Oscar’s passion for bringing people together is a natural progression. Oscar’s Pizza gives guests another reason to gather around the table while carrying the community-minded spirit on which Highland was built. Oscar’s Pizza will serve made-from-scratch thin and crispy pies, salads and shareables, with Guest Experience Director Chris Genua leading development of the concept alongside Head Chef Adam Jones. Genua brings a lifelong obsession with pizza and Southern Italian food to the menu, while Jones brings extensive experience opening concepts and leading high-volume kitchens. Genua, a first-generation Italian American who grew up in Philadelphia, has been making pizza since childhood, starting alongside his grandmother and later with family in Italy. After moving to New York City, he spent 12 years immersed in the city’s pizza and restaurant culture, eventually taking what began as a lifelong passion into a professional setting. His restaurant experience included serving as opening general manager of Brooklyn’s The Double Windsor, where he spent six years and helped develop the food program, before moving to Asheville and leading the pizza concept for White Labs Brewing Co. At Oscar’s Pizza, Genua is drawing on those Philadelphia, New York, and Southern Italian influences to create his take on New Haven-style pizza. “Pizza has always been tied to family for me. I grew up making it with my dad and grandmother in Philadelphia, made it with my family in Italy, and later spent years immersed in the pizza cultures of New York and New Haven,” Genua said. “Oscar’s brings all of those influences together in a thin, crispy, charred pie meant to be shared with friends over a few Highland beers.” Leading the kitchen alongside Genua is Head Chef Adam Jones, a Hickory, North Carolina, native who moved to Asheville to attend culinary school before building his career in kitchens across Asheville, Charleston, Denver, and Dallas. Jones has helped open new restaurant concepts and led teams in high-volume kitchens, developing an approach that balances precision, creativity, and execution at scale. Namesake Oscar Wong was a 54-year-old retired engineer in 1994 when he broke into the beer business. He began brewing Asheville’s first craft beer, Gaelic Amber Ale, on refurbished dairy equipment in the basement of Barley’s, a pub in downtown Asheville. He would become known as the Godfather of Asheville craft beer, paving the way for what would become a vibrant local beer culture and a leading economic driver. Oscar Wong passed away in 2025, leaving an indelible mark on the Asheville community. “He was one of the craft beer pioneers of the American South, and his commitment to high-quality beer was matched by the care he showed for his community, our staff, our family and the people he mentored,” said Leah Wong Ashburn, Wong’s daughter and President & CEO of Highland Brewing. “Oscar’s Pizza is one way that we can keep nourishing our community in his memory.” Oscar’s Pizza pays tribute to its namesake in more personal ways, including on the box. Wong had his first encounter with pizza after immigrating from Jamaica to attend the University of Notre Dame in the 1950s. koreanSummary: 정식품(대표 정연호)이 6일부터 11월 14일까지 헬스케어 플랫폼 ‘닥터다이어리’와 함께 ‘그린비아 만보 걷기 챌린지’를 진행한다.
챌린지는 오는 11월 14일 세계 당뇨병의 날을 맞아 당뇨 환자와 혈당 관리에 관심 있는 소비자들이 일상에서 쉽고 즐겁게 당 관리를 실천할 수 있도록 마련됐다.
참여 방법은 닥터다이어리 앱에 자동 탑재된 만보기 기능을 활용해 하루 만보 걷기 챌린지에 성공하면 ‘그린비아 당 케어’ 이벤트 응모권을 받을 수 있다.
